subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: preparing facts, cause and options first [Thinking]
passage:
Parul: Call with the hospital admin at 3. Go-live moves by three weeks. I'm not calling until I've got my facts straight.
Siddharth: What have you got?
Parul: Cause: the lab-results feed failed on real data, not test data. New date: the 24th. And two ways to soften it: start with the outpatient wing only, or run old and new side by side for a week.
Siddharth: They'll ask why we didn't catch it.
Parul: Probably. Answer: the test data was too clean, and we've added real samples now.
Siddharth: Good. Keep it short.
Parul: Yes. Cause, date, options, then listen.
Siddharth: 👍

qa.q: What was the cause of the delay?
qa.a: The lab-results feed failed on real data, not test data.

qa.q: What might Parul be worried about before the call?
qa.a: Parul is probably worried about being asked why the problem was not caught, which is why Parul prepared an answer.

qa.q: What else could Parul do to make the call go well, and why?
qa.a: Parul could send a short written summary right after the call, because it gives the hospital admin the cause, date and options in one place.

qa.q: How might the hospital admin feel about the news?
qa.a: The hospital admin will probably be worried about patients and staff, but a clear cause, new date and options give something to work with.

grounding: Illustrates preparing the cause, new date and two ways to reduce impact before telling a hospital client that go-live will slip.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: preparing facts, cause and options first [Thinking]
passage:
In the district town of Sagar, Mohit managed the software rollout for a mid-sized hospital. On Thursday he learned that go-live would be three weeks late. The lab machines' data wasn't matching the new system, and fixing the connection would take time.
He had to tell the hospital administrator, Dr Ritu, on Monday. His first impulse was to call right away and just say "delay". He stopped himself. She'll ask why. She'll ask when. She'll ask what it means for patients.
So he spent Friday preparing. The cause, in one sentence: the lab machines send results in an older format. The new date: 14 August. And two ideas to soften the blow: keep the old lab system running in parallel until then, and move the outpatient module live on the original date, since it didn't depend on lab data.
On Monday, Dr Ritu listened, frowned, then said, "Thank you for coming with a plan." They chose both options.

qa.q: What was the new go-live date?
What was Mohit thinking when he stopped himself from calling right away?
qa.a: He was anxious and thinking ahead, knowing Dr Ritu would ask why, when and what it meant for patients.

qa.q: What else could Mohit prepare for such a meeting?
qa.a: He could prepare a short written note of the cause, date and options to leave with Dr Ritu, so the hospital staff can plan too.

qa.q: How does Dr Ritu see the way the news was delivered?
qa.a: Dr Ritu is unhappy about the delay but appreciates that Mohit came with a plan, not just bad news.

grounding: Shows an account lead preparing the cause, the new date and two ways to reduce impact before telling a hospital client that go-live will slip by three weeks.

subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: preparing facts, cause and options first [Thinking]
passage:
Nadia worked as an account lead for a small software firm in Lisbon, and on a Wednesday she found out the new patient records system for a private hospital would go live three weeks late. The data migration from the old system had hit corrupted files.
Her colleague Lucia said, "Call them now, get it over with."
Nadia shook her head. "If I call now, all I can say is 'sorry, it's late'. They'll ask why, and what now, and I won't know."
So she spent the afternoon getting answers. From the engineers: the cause, corrupted files in the older records, and how long cleaning them would take. From that: a new date, 2 October. Then two ideas to soften it: bring the staff training forward so nurses would be ready early, and give the hospital daily progress reports during the delay.
The next morning, she called the hospital director. It was a hard call, but a short one.

qa.q: What was the new date for go-live?
Why did Nadia wait before calling, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She was uneasy about calling with nothing but an apology, and wanted to feel prepared with the cause and a plan.

qa.q: What else could Nadia do after the call?
qa.a: She could send the promised daily progress reports reliably, so the hospital sees the delay being handled.

qa.q: How might the hospital director see the call?
qa.a: The director would still be unhappy about the delay but may feel reassured by the clear cause, new date and options.

grounding: Shows an account lead gathering the cause, new date and two ways to lessen impact before telling a hospital client about a three-week slip.
